cards.front: Recall a key point about S3 Grouped Data
cards.back: Grouped data organises values into class intervals. When class intervals have different widths, we need special techniques to represent them fairly.

cards.front: What should you know about higher tier only?
cards.back: Histograms with unequal class intervals and cumulative frequency graphs are Higher tier topics. You must understand frequency density.

cards.front: What should you know about when class widths are equal?
cards.back: The height of each bar represents the frequency directly. Bars touch each other (no gaps).

cards.front: What should you know about key formula?
cards.back: Frequency Density = Frequency ÷ Class Width The area of each bar represents the frequency, not the height!

cards.front: What should you know about why use frequency density??
cards.back: With unequal intervals, a larger class would unfairly look bigger if we used height. Frequency density makes comparisons fair.

cards.front: What should you know about cumulative frequency?
cards.back: A running total of frequencies. We plot this against the upper class boundary of each interval.

cards.front: What should you know about how to construct?
cards.back: Find the cumulative frequency for each class (add frequencies) Plot points at upper class boundaries Join points with a smooth curve Start from (lower boundary of first class, 0)

cards.front: What should you know about from a cumulative frequency graph?
cards.back: Median (Q2): Go to half the total frequency on y-axis, read across to curve, then down to x-axis Lower Quartile (Q1): Go to quarter of total frequency Upper Quartile (Q3): Go to three-quarters of total frequency

cards.front: Recall a key point about S3 Grouped Data
cards.back: For grouped data problems: (1) For histograms, always calculate frequency density = frequency ÷ class width, (2) Remember: area of bar = frequency, NOT height, (3) For cumulative frequency, plot at UPPER class boundaries, (4) To find median from cumulative frequency graph, go to half the total on y-axis, read across to curve, then down to x-axis, (5) For estimated mean from grouped data, use midpoints: mean = Σ(f × midpoint) ÷ Σf.

cards.front: What should you know about answers?
cards.back: (a) Median at CF=60: read from curve ≈ 64. Q1 at CF=30: ≈ 55. Q3 at CF=90: ≈ 73. IQR = 73−55 = 18. (b) At score 65, read CF ≈ 50. Students passing = 120−50 = 70. (c) Between 60 and 80: CF at 80 = 108, CF at 60 = 48. Students in range = 108−48 = 60 out of 120 = 50%. "Most" means more than 50%, so the claim is borderline — exactly half, not "most".
A range of values grouped together (e.g. 0-10)
Number of items in each class

cards.front: What does Upper Class Boundary mean?
cards.back: The highest value in a class interval
